The Renaissance ("rebirth") was a cultural movement that began in Florence in the 14th century and spread through Italy and then the rest of Europe. It marks the shift from the late Middle Ages to the early modern era [1]. At its core was humanism. Scholars such as Petrarch worked to recover ancient Greek and Roman texts and stressed what human beings could achieve [1].

Several forces drove it. After the Black Death (1348–50), survivors' labour was worth more and many inherited property, which reshaped the economy. Greek scholars fleeing the fall of Constantinople in 1453 brought classical manuscripts west. Gutenberg's printing press, from around 1440, made books far cheaper and easier to spread. Wealthy patrons like Florence's Medici family paid for artists' work [1].

In art, figures like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael mastered perspective, anatomy and realistic emotion [1]. The period also brought the Age of Discovery and Copernicus's sun-centred astronomy, which challenged older authorities like Ptolemy [1]. As the movement spread north, it helped cause the Protestant Reformation: humanist study of the Bible's original texts shaped Martin Luther's challenge to the Church in 1517 [1]. The Italian High Renaissance is usually said to end with the Sack of Rome in 1527, but its influence lasted into the 17th century across Europe [1].
